lines.text: Whether to look inside a query was last topic's question. Now a different one: before a query runs at all, how does the planner guess how many rows it will touch?
Watch the two readouts. One guess lands almost on the real count once the query actually runs. The other guess is off by more than double.
Same table. Same machinery that produced both guesses. So why does only one of them hold up?
Here are two separate conditions on the same table. One matches about one row in six. The other matches more than a third of the rows.
If the planner treats them as having nothing to do with each other, what fraction does it expect when both conditions are required at once?
Multiply the two, add them, or just take the smaller one?
Multiply them. About one sixth times a bit more than a third lands close to one in seventeen.
That is exactly what treating the conditions as unrelated means: whatever one matches has nothing to do with whatever the other matches, so their chances multiply.
Whether that assumption is actually true for these two columns is the real question, and it is not.
The guess really does land where multiplying predicts: a little under six in a hundred.
But watch the real count once the query runs. It lands past twice that.
The planner's arithmetic was not the problem. Its assumption was: these two columns move together, and nothing about multiplying separate chances can see that.
So where does a guess come from in the first place? One catalog keeps a cheap running total: how many rows a table has, rescaled to its current size without ever reading the table.
A second, harder catalog keeps the shape of each column: the spread of values, which ones repeat often, roughly how many distinct values exist.
Its own documentation calls that second catalog approximate even right after it is refreshed. Everything from here is about that harder number.
Take a numeric column and ask for everything above a cutoff. The column's whole range has been cut into a hundred equal slices, each holding the same share of rows.
Watch the pointer travel along the line and settle inside one slice. Every full slice before it counts completely; the slice it lands in counts only its fraction.
Whole slices plus a fraction of one more, out of a hundred, is the guess — and here it lands within about one part in a hundred of the real count.
A different kind of column: six possible outcomes, and one of them, a refund, is rare — barely more than one row in sixty.
When a value is common enough to be tracked by name, the catalog already knows exactly how often it shows up in the sample. Lock onto the thin bar.
Asking for that one outcome doesn't need a slice or a formula at all. The measured share is the guess.
Now ask for a value that isn't common enough to be tracked by name. The catalog knows the combined share taken by every value it does track.
Whatever share is left over gets divided evenly across every other distinct value that wasn't tracked, as if each of them were exactly as common as the rest.
That even division is a second assumption, doing the same job the slices did a moment ago: standing in for a real measurement with a guess.
Back to the two columns that move together. One command tells the planner to measure them as a pair instead of separately, watching for exactly this kind of dependence.
After that command runs and the catalog is refreshed, the same query's guess jumps from roughly half of the real count to within about one part in a hundred of it.
Nothing about the arithmetic changed. What changed is that the planner now has an actual joint measurement instead of an assumption about two unrelated columns.
A large batch of new rows lands all at once, every one sharing the same outcome for a column the planner already has stale measurements for, and nobody refreshes the catalog yet.
Does the planner's guess for that outcome notice the new rows arrived at all?
Does it notice fully, not at all, or only part of what changed?

tolerated.line: Does the planner's guess for that outcome notice the new rows arrived at all?

lines.text: Only part. The cheap running total of how many rows exist updates on its own, scaled to the table's new size.
But the shape — how common each outcome actually is now — does not update until the harder catalog is refreshed. That refresh is a separate, deliberate step.
So the guess undercounts: it has the new total, but still the old mix.
Before the refresh, the guess lands well under the real count once the query runs — off by about sixty percent.
One refresh later, with no other change at all, the same guess lands within less than half a percent of the real count.
Both failures just shown are guesses feeding into a larger plan, and a larger plan is usually more than one step.
Line up this topic's two measured misses — the unrelated-columns guess and the stale-shape guess — as if the same plan depended on both.
They don't cancel each other out. They compound, landing well past three times off, because each one feeds the next step as if it were simply true.
The planner's own documentation admits plainly that two different ways of sizing the same join can land far apart.
Every formula shown so far is still a fixed recipe a person designed years ago, applied to a small sample.
One active line of research trains a model directly on real data and real queries instead, aimed specifically at the kind of related-column failure this topic just measured.
That line of work is still a research direction, not this topic's mechanism — more of it waits in the deep dive.

Three questions, before trusting the first number a plan shows you: do the columns in the condition actually move together? When was the harder catalog last refreshed? And is this guess itself about to feed into another step?
An estimate only matters once something compares it against the alternatives — and that comparison, the actual price of a plan, is next.
A value tracked by name shows up in two out of every hundred rows, on a table of half a million rows.
How many rows should the planner expect this condition to match?
Ten, a hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand?
Ten thousand. Two in a hundred of half a million.
A value tracked by name gets its share read straight from the catalog and multiplied by the row count — no slice, no leftover division.
Two separate conditions on columns that actually move together are each guessed at around one in five, treated as unrelated to each other.
What is the real risk hiding inside that guess?
Too high, too low, or no risk at all?

tolerated.line: What is the real risk hiding inside that guess?

lines.text: Too low. Columns that move together overlap more than treating them as unrelated predicts.
The multiplied guess undershoots the real, larger overlap — the same failure this topic measured directly, at about double.
